name: Taking of southwestern Washington without a treaty; Chehalis Reservation set apart by order of the Secretary of the Interior, July 8, 1864
citation: No treaty or statute; Secretary of the Interior's approval of the Chehalis reserve, July 8, 1864 (Royce, schedule entry 458)
nations: Upper Chehalis and Lower Chehalis (Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation)
promises: There was no treaty and so no promise. Royce's schedule records that these tribes claimed the country between the Nisqually and Quinault territory on the north, the Cascade Mountains on the east and the Columbia River on the south, and that the United States took possession of it without any treaty.

The only provision made was a small reserve: on July 8, 1864 the Secretary of the Interior approved setting aside 4,224.63 acres as a reservation for the Chehalis, per the Indian Claims Commission's findings. A second reserve, at Shoalwater Bay, followed by executive order of September 22, 1866.

breaches.what: After the Court of Claims reversed its first dismissal, the Indian Claims Commission held that the Upper Chehalis and Lower Chehalis held Indian title to their lands and that the United States acquired that title on March 3, 1855, the day treaty talks ended, without their consent and without paying for it.

breaches.what: The Chehalis Tribe says that at the February 1855 treaty council the government proposed moving the Chehalis to a reservation far north of their homeland, no agreement was reached, a treaty was never signed, and its reservation came by executive order in July 1864.

landTaken: The Commission found the Lower Chehalis held Indian title to 517,700 acres and the Upper Chehalis to 320,500 acres, 838,200 acres in all (Docket 237, 1963 findings). The Chinook and Clatsop tract contained 76,639 acres of dry land (Docket 234, 1970).
compensation: Chehalis: a compromise final judgment of $754,380.00 (Docket 237, 1963). Lower Band of Chinook and Clatsop: final award of $48,692.05 (Docket 234, November 4, 1970). The Commission also dismissed, in 1956, a claim for 3,753.63 acres of the Chehalis Reservation restored to the public domain in 1886, finding the land had been allotted and patented to Indians living on it; the Court of Claims did not disturb that part.
today: The Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation live on the reservation near Oakville set apart in 1864 and describe themselves as an executive-order tribe, not a treaty tribe.

nationVoice.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation
nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's own history says the 1855 council on the Chehalis River broke down after three days because the government wanted to move the Chehalis far north of their villages, that no treaty was ever signed, and that its reservation in Upper Chehalis territory was made by executive order in 1864.

openQuestions: treaties.json: this is not a cession agreement. The 1864-07-08 date is the Secretary of the Interior's approval of the Chehalis reserve; Royce says the United States took the territory without any treaty. The ICC dated the Chehalis taking to March 3, 1855.

treaties.json: Royce's tribe list includes Klatsop (Clatsop), whose lands the ICC placed in Oregon, south of the Columbia; Royce 458's description stops at the Columbia. Whether the Chinook tract valued in Docket 234 falls inside Royce 458 was not checked on the map; the ICC dated that taking to August 1851, tied to the unratified Tansy Point treaties.
Klikitat lands are not covered here; the Klikitat were party to the 1855 Yakama treaty and their claims were pursued with the Yakama. Not checked.
No Chinook Indian Nation or Shoalwater Bay Tribe account was opened for this file.

plain.promised: Nothing was promised. There was no treaty. The United States took the country north of the Columbia River without one, and in 1864 set aside a small reservation for the Chehalis.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1960 that the United States took Chehalis land in 1855 without consent or payment, and in 1970 that the price paid for Chinook and Clatsop land was unconscionable.
plain.today: The Chehalis claim was settled by compromise for $754,380 in 1963; the Chinook and Clatsop were awarded $48,692.05 in 1970. The Chehalis Tribe says a treaty was never signed.
